blocks.text: A Fenwick Tree, also known as a Binary Indexed Tree (BIT), is a compact and efficient data structure used to perform prefix sum and range sum queries while also supporting point updates in O(log n) time.
It overcomes the biggest limitation of the simple prefix sum approach: updating an element is no longer O(n).
With a Fenwick Tree, both:

items: Point Update: Update arr[i]
Range Sum Query: Find the sum of elements in a range [l, r]

blocks.text: can be performed efficiently in O(log n) time, making it ideal for problems involving frequent updates and queries on an array.

content.title: 1. The Problem with Plain Prefix Sum

blocks.text: Prefix Sum is excellent when the array is static. Once the prefix array is built, any range sum can be answered in O(1)time.
The problem begins when the array changes.

If even a single element is updated, every prefix value after that index becomes invalid and must be recalculated. In the worst case, this means rebuilding almost the entire prefix array, which takes O(n) time.
So, while Prefix Sum gives:

items: Range Sum Query: O(1)
Point Update: O(n)

blocks.text: it performs poorly in problems that involve frequent updates and frequent queries.

This is exactly where the Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree) comes in. Instead of storing complete prefix sums, it stores carefully chosen partial sums, allowing both operations to be performed efficiently:

items: Range Sum Query: O(log n)
Point Update: O(log n)

blocks.text: Fenwick Tree sacrifices a little query speed in exchange for dramatically faster updates, making it the ideal choice whenever a problem requires repeatedly updating elements and querying range sums on the same array.

content.title: 2. The Core Idea: Partial Sums Through Binary Representation

blocks.text: A Fenwick Tree does not store the prefix sum for every index. Instead, each position stores the sum of a specific block of elements. The size of this block is determined by the lowest set bit in the index's binary representation.
This lowest set bit is computed as:
The value of lowbit(i) tells us how many elements index i is responsible for.
For example:

items: i = 6 (110₂) → lowbit = 2 → stores the sum of the last 2 elements, covering [5, 6]
i = 8 (1000₂) → lowbit = 8 → stores the sum of the last 8 elements, covering [1, 8]
i = 12 (1100₂) → lowbit = 4 → stores the sum of the last 4 elements, covering [9, 12]
i = 7 (111₂) → lowbit = 1 → stores only [7, 7]

blocks.text: In general, index i stores the sum of the range:
Because these ranges are carefully chosen and overlap in a structured way, a Fenwick Tree can move between ranges by simply adding or subtracting lowbit(i).
This clever use of binary representation is what allows both updates and prefix sum queries to run in O(log n) time.

content.title: 3. What Each Fenwick Tree Index Stores

blocks.text: A common misconception is that a Fenwick Tree stores every prefix sum. It doesn't.
Instead, each index stores the sum of a specific range of elements, and the size of that range is determined by:
For an array of 8 elements, the ranges stored are:
Why these ranges?
The rule is:

codes.javascript:
tree[i] stores the sum of:
[i - lowbit(i) + 1, i]

blocks.text: For example:

items: tree[6] → lowbit(6) = 2Stores sum of [5,6]
tree[4] → lowbit(4) = 4Stores sum of [1,4]
tree[8] → lowbit(8) = 8Stores sum of [1,8]

blocks.text: Notice something interesting:

items: Some nodes store just one element.
Some store 2 elements.
Some store 4 elements.
Some store 8 elements.

blocks.text: The ranges become larger as the lowest set bit becomes larger.
Why is this useful?
These ranges are carefully designed so that:

items: Querying a prefix sum can be done by jumping through a few ranges and adding their sums.
Updating an element can be done by updating only the ranges that contain that element.

blocks.text: Because each jump removes or adds one set bit from the index, both operations take only:
This clever arrangement of overlapping ranges is the entire reason why a Fenwick Tree supports both updates and queries efficiently.

content.title: 4. Why this works ( The update path )

blocks.text: When you update arr[5], you don't need to touch every index.
You only need to update the indices whose range includes 5: index 5, then index 6 (since 6's range [5,6] includes 5), then index 8 (since 8's range [1,8] includes 5).
Each step jumps forward using i += lowbit(i).

codes.javascript:
Update arr[5]:

  i = 5  → update tree[5]  → next: i += lowbit(5) = 5+1 = 6
  i = 6  → update tree[6]  → next: i += lowbit(6) = 6+2 = 8
  i = 8  → update tree[8]  → next: i += lowbit(8) = 8+8 = 16 (out of bounds, stop)

Only 3 nodes touched instead of rebuilding the whole array — O(log n)

content.title: 5. Why this works ( The query path )

blocks.text: To get the prefix sum up to index 7, you don't sum all 7 elements one by one. You jump backward using i -= lowbit(i), accumulating ranges until you reach 0.

codes.javascript:
Query prefix sum up to index 7:

  i = 7  → add tree[7] (covers [7,7]) → next: i -= lowbit(7) = 7-1 = 6
  i = 6  → add tree[6] (covers [5,6]) → next: i -= lowbit(6) = 6-2 = 4
  i = 4  → add tree[4] (covers [1,4]) → next: i -= lowbit(4) = 4-4 = 0 (stop)

Total: tree[7] + tree[6] + tree[4] = sum of arr[1..7]
Only 3 additions instead of 7 — O(log n)

items: Update goes UP the tree adding lowbit.
Query goes DOWN the tree subtracting lowbit.

blocks.text: Both take at most O(log n) steps since the number of set bits in any number is at most log n.

Building from an existing array
The simplest build: call update(i, arr[i]) for every element O(n log n). A faster O(n) build exists but is rarely needed in interviews.

Fenwick Tree is the sweet spot for sum/XOR/count queries with updates much simpler to code than a Segment Tree. Use Segment Tree only when you need range updates, min/max queries, or more complex range operations.

items: Point update, range query: The standard form shown above. Update one element, query a sum range.
Range update, point query: Use a difference array trick: update(l, +val) and update(r+1, -val). Query is just a prefix sum lookup.
Range update, range query: Requires two Fenwick Trees working together with a formula combining them. More advanced, rarely needed.
2D Fenwick Tree: Nested update/query loops over both dimensions. Used for 2D range sum with point updates O(log n × log m).
Counting inversions: Use Fenwick Tree to count, for each element, how many smaller elements appeared before it classic O(n log n) inversion count.
Order statistics / rank queries: Use index = value (after coordinate compression) to answer "how many elements ≤ x have I seen so far" queries.

blocks.text: We process the array from right to left. For each element, the Fenwick Tree stores the frequency of elements we've already seen (i.e., elements to its right).query(r - 1)gives the number of smaller elements on the right, which directly contributes to the inversion count.
Coordinate compression is used because Fenwick Tree indices must lie in the range1...n.

blocks.text: This uses the difference array trick. Instead of updating every element in[l, r], we addvalatland-valatr + 1. The prefix sum automatically propagates the update to all indices in the range, making each range update O(log n) instead of O(n).

Using 0-indexed Fenwick Tree i & (-i) breaks at index 0. Always use 1-indexed.
Confusing tree[i] with arr[i] the Fenwick tree array stores partial sums, not original values. Don't read tree[i] expecting arr[i].
Off-by-one in range queries remember rangeQuery(l, r) = query(r) - query(l-1), not query(r) - query(l).
Forgetting coordinate compression when values are large or negative Fenwick Tree indices must be positive and bounded.
Using Fenwick Tree when you need min/max instead of sum Fenwick Tree's subtraction trick only works for invertible operations like sum and XOR, not min/max.
Updating with the new value instead of the delta update(i, delta) expects the change amount, not the new total.
